q: Where is a primary oocyte arrested until its follicle's LH surge?
x: Prophase I. Oocytes enter meiosis I in the fetal ovary and stay paused there, 2N with 4C of DNA, until the LH surge of their own cycle restarts division.

w.Metaphase II: Metaphase II is the second pause, reached only after the surge completes meiosis I. It lasts from ovulation until fertilization.
w.Anaphase I: Anaphase I is the moment homologous chromosomes separate after the surge. It takes minutes and is where nondisjunction errors appear.
w.Telophase I: Telophase I is the brief end of meiosis I, when the first polar body pinches off just before ovulation.
w.Prophase II: Prophase II is crossed quickly on the way to metaphase II; the secondary oocyte never rests there.

pt.say: The primary oocyte band says arrested in prophase I, from fetal life until the LH surge.

q: Which cell leaves the follicle at ovulation?
x: A secondary oocyte, arrested in metaphase II with its first polar body beside it; it becomes a mature ovum only if a sperm enters and meiosis II finishes.

w.Primary oocyte: The primary oocyte finishes meiosis I in response to the LH surge before the follicle ruptures, so the cell that leaves is already secondary.
w.Mature ovum: A true ovum exists only after sperm entry completes meiosis II and expels the second polar body; an unfertilized egg never reaches that stage.
w.Oogonium: Oogonia are the mitotic precursors in the fetal ovary; all of them have entered meiosis or died before birth.
w.Zygote: A zygote forms after fertilization in the ampulla, hours after ovulation, when the two pronuclei combine.

pt.say: The bottom box states it: ovulation releases a secondary oocyte still arrested in metaphase II.

q: What is the ploidy and DNA content of a primary oocyte?
x: 2N, 4C. The primary oocyte replicated its DNA before entering meiosis I, so it keeps the diploid chromosome number with double the DNA until the first division halves it.

w.2N, 2C: This describes an oogonium or any resting body cell before DNA replication, not a cell paused partway through meiosis I.
w.1N, 2C: This is the secondary oocyte after meiosis I halves the chromosome number while each chromosome still carries two chromatids.
w.1N, 1C: This is the final haploid state of an ovum or spermatid, after meiosis II separates the sister chromatids.
w.4N, 4C: Tetraploid cells carry four chromosome sets; meiosis replicates DNA once but never doubles the number of chromosome sets.

hl: Primary oocyte: arrested in prophase I (2N, 4C)
pt.say: The primary oocyte band is labeled 2N, 4C: diploid with replicated DNA.

q: Which follicle cell supplies androstenedione to the granulosa cells?
x: Theca interna cells. LH drives them to convert LDL cholesterol into androstenedione, which crosses the basement membrane for granulosa aromatase to turn into estradiol.

w.Oocyte: The oocyte directs follicle growth with signals but has no steroid enzymes to make androgens.
w.Cumulus cell: Cumulus cells are granulosa cells around the oocyte; like other granulosa cells they aromatize androgen rather than make it.
w.Surface epithelial cell: The surface epithelium is a mesothelial covering and the origin of epithelial ovarian tumors. It is not a steroid source.
w.Leydig cell: Leydig cells are the testicular androgen-making cells. The ovarian follicle uses theca interna cells for this job.

pt.say: The theca interna cell box shows cholesterol turning into androstenedione under LH, then crossing the membrane.

q: Which enzyme does FSH switch on in granulosa cells?
x: Aromatase. FSH induces aromatase in granulosa cells, which converts androstenedione to estrone and testosterone to estradiol; this is the FSH half of the two-cell model.

w.17α-hydroxylase: 17α-hydroxylase is a theca enzyme driven by LH that builds androgens; granulosa cells lack it.
w.Cholesterol desmolase: Desmolase performs side-chain cleavage, the first step of every steroid pathway, and is driven by LH in theca cells.
w.5α-reductase: 5α-reductase turns testosterone into DHT in prostate and genital skin, making a stronger androgen rather than an estrogen.
w.3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase: This enzyme converts pregnenolone to progesterone and DHEA to androstenedione early in the pathway; FSH does not specifically induce it for estrogen synthesis.

pt.say: In the granulosa cell box, the FSH receptor switches on aromatase, turning theca androgen into estrogen.

x: Estrone. Once the follicles are gone, most estrogen comes from aromatase in adipose tissue converting androstenedione to estrone, so heavier women make more of it.

w.Estradiol: Estradiol is the potent follicular estrogen of the reproductive years; its production collapses when the follicle pool is exhausted.
w.Estriol: Estriol is the weak placental estrogen of pregnancy, made from fetal adrenal precursors.
w.Ethinyl estradiol: Ethinyl estradiol is the synthetic estrogen in most combined oral contraceptives, not a hormone the body makes.
w.Androstenedione: Androstenedione is the androgen that fat converts into estrone. It is a precursor, not an estrogen.

pt.say: The outside-the-ovary box shows adipose aromatase making estrone by peripheral conversion, the main estrogen after menopause.

q: Which hormone surge causes ovulation about 36 hours after it begins?
x: LH. Sustained high estradiol switches the pituitary to positive feedback; the LH surge restarts meiosis I, activates proteases that open the follicle wall and luteinizes its cells.

w.FSH: FSH rises a little with LH at mid-cycle, but its main job is earlier: recruiting follicles and inducing granulosa aromatase.
w.Estradiol: Estradiol sets off the surge by flipping feedback, but estradiol itself does not rupture the follicle; the LH it releases does.
w.Progesterone: Progesterone climbs after ovulation from the corpus luteum and suppresses further surges during the luteal phase.
w.Prolactin: High prolactin suppresses GnRH pulses, which blocks ovulation rather than triggering it.

pt.say: The LH surge peaks just before the ovulation line; ovulation follows about 36 hours after it begins.

q: Which phase of the ovarian cycle stays close to 14 days long?
x: The luteal phase. The corpus luteum has a built-in lifespan of about 14 days unless hCG rescues it, so cycle length varies mainly in the follicular phase.

w.Follicular phase: Follicle selection takes a variable time, so the follicular phase stretches or shrinks and sets total cycle length.
w.Menstrual phase: Menstrual flow lasts about three to seven days and overlaps the start of the follicular phase.
w.Proliferative phase: Proliferative is the endometrial name for the follicular half, so it varies just as much.
w.Ovulatory phase: Ovulation is a single event about 36 hours after the surge begins, not a two-week stretch of the cycle.

pt.say: The ovarian phase bar labels the luteal phase about 14 days, while the follicular phase length varies.

q: On which day of a 28-day cycle does progesterone peak?
x: Day 21, about seven days after ovulation, when the corpus luteum is fully active. That is why a mid-luteal progesterone, drawn a week before menses, confirms ovulation.

w.Day 14: Day 14 is ovulation; progesterone is only beginning to rise as the follicle cells luteinize.
w.Day 7: Day 7 is mid-follicular; estradiol is climbing and progesterone is at its lowest.
w.Day 1: Day 1 is the start of menses, triggered by the fall of progesterone at the end of the previous cycle.
w.Day 28: By day 28 the corpus luteum has regressed and progesterone has fallen, which is what brings on menses.

pt.say: Progesterone peaks mid-luteal, over day 21 on the axis, a week after ovulation.

q: Which endometrial finding is the first sign of progesterone effect?
x: Subnuclear glycogen vacuoles appear about two days after ovulation, the earliest secretory change; luminal secretion, edema and predecidual cells follow over the next 12 days.

w.Mitoses in straight glands: Mitoses in straight tubular glands are the estradiol-driven proliferative pattern seen before ovulation.
w.Stromal edema: Stromal edema peaks about a week after ovulation, near implantation, after the vacuoles have moved upward.
w.Predecidual cells: Predecidual change appears around spiral arteries late in the luteal phase, just before menses or implantation.
w.Luminal secretions: Secretions fill gland lumens in the mid-luteal phase, once the vacuoles have discharged above the nuclei.

pt.say: On the day clock, subnuclear vacuoles come first, at +2 days: the earliest sign of progesterone, before luminal secretions, stromal edema and predecidual cells appear.

q: Which endometrial layer regenerates the lining after each menses?
x: The stratum basalis, fed by straight arteries, is not shed; its glands and stroma rebuild the functionalis each cycle, and removing it by curettage causes Asherman adhesions.

w.Stratum functionalis: The functionalis, fed by spiral arteries, is the layer that is shed, so it cannot regenerate itself.
w.Myometrium: The myometrium is smooth muscle beneath the endometrium; it contracts during menses but never makes new glands.
w.Perimetrium: The perimetrium is the outer serosal coat of the uterus, far from the cavity lining.
w.Mesometrium: The mesometrium is the part of the broad ligament that wraps the uterus. It lies outside the uterus and does not regrow the lining.

pt.say: The stratum basalis is never shed: fed by straight arteries, it regrows the functionalis each cycle, and curettage through it causes Asherman syndrome.

q: What cervical mucus pattern appears just before ovulation?
x: Thin, watery and stretchy. Peak estradiol makes abundant mucus that pulls into long strands (spinnbarkeit) and ferns on a slide, letting sperm swim through in the fertile window.

w.Thick and scant: Thick, scant mucus is the progesterone pattern of the luteal phase and of progestin contraceptives, and it blocks sperm.
w.Dry and sticky: Dry, sticky mucus is typical just after menses, when estradiol is still low and the fertile window has not opened.
w.Purulent and yellow: Purulent yellow discharge suggests cervicitis, such as gonorrhea or chlamydia, rather than a hormonal phase.
w.Blood-streaked: Blood streaks suggest menses, a cervical lesion or trauma, not the normal ovulatory mucus change.

pt.say: The endocervix row shows mucinous cells making thin, watery, stretchy mucus at peak estradiol, the fertile pattern just before ovulation.

x: Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium covers the ectocervix and vagina; mucinous columnar cells line the endocervix, and dysplasia begins in the transformation zone where the two meet.

w.Mucinous simple columnar: Mucinous columnar cells line the endocervical canal and make the mucus that estradiol thins and progesterone thickens.
w.Ciliated simple columnar: Ciliated columnar cells line the fallopian tube, where their beating moves the oocyte toward the uterus.
w.Keratinized stratified squamous: Keratinized squamous epithelium covers skin and the outer vulva, not the moist ectocervix.
w.Transitional epithelium: Transitional epithelium, or urothelium, lines the bladder and ureters rather than the genital tract.

pt.say: The ectocervix row reads nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, continuous with the vagina; mucinous columnar cells begin only at the endocervix.

q: What causes the mid-cycle pain called mittelschmerz?
x: Follicle rupture at ovulation. Fluid or blood released when the follicle opens irritates the peritoneum, giving brief one-sided lower abdominal pain in the middle of the cycle.

w.Corpus luteum regression: Luteolysis happens quietly at the end of the luteal phase and leads to menses, not to mid-cycle pain.
w.Prostaglandin-driven uterine cramps: Prostaglandin cramps are primary dysmenorrhea at the start of menses, two weeks away from mid-cycle.
w.Endometrial implants on the peritoneum: Implants cause endometriosis pain, usually with menses, intercourse or defecation, often worsening over years.
w.Ovarian torsion: Torsion causes sudden severe pain with nausea and needs surgery; it is an emergency, not a monthly normal event.

pt.say: The ovary row ties mittelschmerz to follicle rupture: the released fluid or blood irritates the peritoneum and gives brief one-sided pain in the middle of the cycle.
